\Section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:evaluation}

The evaluation compares along two dimensions.
\emph{Arm against arm} (Sec.~\ref{sec:eval-arms}) holds the model fixed and varies the tactic: \textit{agent-only}, \textit{hybrid-guided}, and \textit{hybrid-flexible}, run under the same conditions.
\emph{Model against model} (Sec.~\ref{sec:eval-models}) repeats the design with two further models and asks how the contribution of \WP changes with the model.
All rounds share the corpus, the scoring, and the cost accounting described first.

\SubSection{Setup}
\label{sec:eval-setup}

\Paragraph{Corpus}
The corpus is drawn from \Anon{Etna, the private Move code of the perpetual trading system Decibel}{the private Move code of a production perpetual trading system}: 23 targets from it, two from a public Move library that carry no upstream specification, and two written for the corpus.
A private codebase matters here: the model cannot have seen these functions, or any specification of them, during training, so a contract has to be inferred rather than recalled.
Every candidate is classified by the features (strata) its contract has to account for --- loops and accumulators, early returns and breaks, arithmetic overflow and underflow, casts and truncation, mutable references and in-place permutation, function values, quantifiers, composition through a callee's contract, and others, 38 in all.
A target is admitted only if it proves within seconds against a hand-written reference specification, and before the round three \emph{mutants} are authored per target --- patches to the implementation, one per obligation the contract has to pin --- each shown to be killed by the reference.
Twenty targets are selected to cover all 38 features across 15 modules, 10 of them with loops; three are deliberately guessable as controls, and five near-duplicates are held back.
With 3 arms and 4 replicates, a model round has \textbf{240 cells}.

\Paragraph{Arms and models}
The three tactics of Sec.~\ref{sec:skills} run as arms that differ only in the rendered plugin: the reference material is byte-identical, and in agent-only the \WP tool is absent rather than discouraged.
Three rounds use three models: Opus~5 at the highest effort setting through the Claude Code SDK, and Sol~5.6 and Terra~5.6 at high effort through the Codex CLI, with the same plugin rendered for each.
\TODO{wg}{The Terra~5.6 round is pending; its rows and table currently hold GLM~5.3 data (maximum effort, Claude Code SDK against an Anthropic-compatible endpoint) as a placeholder, marked $^\dagger$.}
Each session has a budget of 100--180k output tokens, one hour of wall time, and 40 seconds of solver time per verification condition.

\Paragraph{Scoring}
A cell reaches \emph{operational success} when a judge outside the agent's workspace confirms that the package compiles, the requested scope verifies, no weakening construct is present --- |pragma verify = false|, partial abort contracts, vacuous postconditions, invented preconditions --- the bytecode is unchanged, and the required contract categories are present.
The agent's own claim is never a score.
In some rounds the controller also applied a visible set of mutants after the agent's first attempt and, if one survived, handed the contract back for strengthening; whether it did so varied between rounds, and the agent was never told a second attempt might follow.
Every round is therefore read the same way: a cell's outcome is the judge's verdict at the end of the agent's \emph{first attempt}, and its cost is what the agent spent up to then; later strengthening turns are not counted anywhere, and a contract that survived a visible mutant at the first attempt is a \emph{weak contract}, a failure.
Operational success is necessary but weak: a vaguer contract passes it more easily.
Completeness --- postconditions as strong as the behavior --- has no deductive check in general; \WP guarantees it only given complete loop invariants and callee contracts, and warns when it cannot, a mechanism the agent-only arm lacks.
The second level is therefore \emph{mutation adequacy}: after the round, each held-out mutant is applied to the implementation and the prover rerun against the inferred specification.
A mutant that still verifies has survived; a cell is \emph{complete} when its first attempt succeeded and killed every held-out mutant.
Held-out scoring has finished for the Opus~5 round and is in progress for the other two.

\Paragraph{Cost}
Costs are in US dollars at each model's published prices at the time of its round, recomputed from the recorded token counters rather than taken from the harness's estimate.
Per million tokens, Opus~5 is \$5 uncached input, \$0.50 cache read, \$10 or \$6.25 cache write, and \$25 output; Sol~5.6 is \$4 uncached input, \$0.40 cached input, \$5 cache write, and \$20 output; Terra~5.6 is \$2, \$0.20, \$2.50, and \$12.
Thinking counts as output for all three.

\SubSection{Arm against Arm}
\label{sec:eval-arms}

Table~\ref{tab:summary} summarizes all rounds; Tables~\ref{tab:opus}--\ref{tab:terra} in the appendix give every target.
Under Opus~5, the hybrids succeeded at the first attempt in all 80 cells each and every one of those killed every held-out mutant.
Agent-only failed 4 of its 80: all four replicates of |QP-part-025|, the in-place permutation, produced at the first attempt a contract that pinned where the partition point lands but not what the vector contains, and a visible mutant survived it.
That is the completeness effect the mechanical baseline is meant to buy, and it lands on the one target whose contract has to characterize a whole data structure.

Cost goes the other way.
In the task-weighted mean, hybrid-guided costs 1.29$\times$ agent-only and hybrid-flexible 1.27$\times$; 95\% percentile bootstrap intervals, holding the 20 tasks fixed and resampling four replicate blocks within each task with the three arms kept together (100,000 draws), are [1.22, 1.37] and [1.20, 1.35].
The hybrids are cheaper on only 5 and 1 of the 20 targets --- |TS-trial-019| under hybrid-guided at 54\% is the largest saving --- and cost most on the function-value target |SM-select-022| (2.0$\times$ and 1.5$\times$) and the lemma target |BA-base-012| (1.5$\times$ and 1.3$\times$).
The |QP-part-025| comparison is not a cost comparison: agent-only's cheap cells there are failed first attempts.

The mechanism is visible in the token and tool counts.
The hybrids process two thirds more input (546k and 502k against 328k per cell) and emit a fifth more output (10.6k and 10.8k against 9.0k): the \WP output and its simplification enter the context and are re-read on every turn, and at cache-read prices that is where the extra cost lies.
They also make more verify calls (160 and 174 against 105) on top of their 150 and 108 \WP calls, and more edits (182 and 177 against 131).

\SubSection{Model against Model}
\label{sec:eval-models}

Under Sol~5.6 the picture shifts.
The hybrids again succeeded at the first attempt in all 80 cells each, and agent-only failed 3 with a weak contract.
At a near-identical price list, Sol~5.6 spends less per cell than Opus~5 in every arm (\$0.52 against \$0.69 for agent-only), because it emits two thirds of the output tokens; and here \WP pays: hybrid-guided and hybrid-flexible cost 0.95$\times$ and 0.94$\times$ agent-only, [0.85, 1.05] and [0.84, 1.04], and are cheaper on 13 and 15 of the 20 targets.
The saving is spread rather than concentrated --- a third to a half off on the small arithmetic contracts (|VS-shares-002|, |VS-contrib-003|, |PM-curve-027|, |BK-bucket-016|) --- and the two targets that cost the hybrids most under Opus~5 cost them most here too: |QP-part-025| at 1.5$\times$ and 1.2$\times$, |BA-base-012| at 1.4$\times$ under hybrid-guided.
The hybrids' input volume is no longer higher than agent-only's (450k and 444k against 479k), because the unaided model reads more of the package instead.

Terra~5.6, the mid-tier model of the same family at a third of Sol's price list, is expected to lean on \WP most: hybrid-guided costs 0.X$\times$ agent-only [0.X, 0.X] and hybrid-flexible 0.X$\times$ [0.X, 0.X], cheaper on X and X of the 20 targets, and agent-only fails X cells at the first attempt against none for the hybrids.
\TODO{wg}{Terra~5.6 round pending; the rows marked $^\dagger$ in Table~\ref{tab:summary} and Table~\ref{tab:terra} hold GLM~5.3 data as a placeholder. Fill in the 0.X figures, then refresh the Sol~5.6 scoring.}

Since each model is priced at its own schedule, the comparison across models is between the within-model ratios, not the dollars.
Read together, the rounds separate two contributions of \WP.
The first is completeness, and it does not depend on the model: in every round the success rate with \WP is higher.
Agent-only left a weak contract at the first attempt in 7 of 160 cells under Opus~5 and Sol~5.6 and X under Terra~5.6, the hybrids in none, and the failures sit on the targets whose contract has to pin down a data structure.
The second is cost, and there different models make different use of the tool: \WP is not a fixed saving but a trade of exact contracts for context, and a model that writes the invariant unaided and re-reads a large context pays for it (Opus~5, 1.3$\times$), a model that reads more and writes less recovers it (Sol~5.6, 0.95$\times$), and a smaller model that would otherwise search recovers more (Terra~5.6, 0.X$\times$).
The Sol~5.6 intervals include parity, so its size is indicative; the spread across the three models is the finding.
